newsitem.title: USA: UPS strike will hit U.S. economy, affect millions.
newsitem.headline: UPS strike will hit U.S. economy, affect millions.

text.p: The strike by hundreds of thousands of United Parcel Service package sorters, loaders and drivers will affect millions of customers across the country and hurt the whole U.S. economy.

UPS, the largest U.S. parcel carrier, handles 12 million packages a day and employs more than 300,000 people in the United States -- 185,000 of whom are represented by the Teamsters, including package sorters, loaders and drivers.
The Teamsters union walked out on last-ditch contract talks on Sunday and began a strike at midnight.
The Independent Pilots Association is backing the strike and said its 2,000 UPS pilots also would refuse to work.
"The impact on the economy is going to be 5 percent of GNP (gross national product) not moving," said company spokeswoman Gina Ellrich.
The White House has been keeping close tabs on the negotiations, but spokesman Barry Toiv said President Bill Clinton did not plan to intervene at this time.
"At this time, the administration does not believe that the standard for intervention under the Taft-Hartley Act has been met," Toiv said.

Clinton intervened under the Railway Labour Act to end an American Airlines strike minutes after it began earlier this year. But, to halt a UPS walkout, Clinton would have to use the cumbersome and time-consuming Taft-Hartley law, which has not been used since the 1950s, to order a mediation board to settle the dispute, the administration official said.
"It would take a pretty severe national economic dislocation to create the conditions under which we could intervene under the Taft-Hartley Act," said one official, who asked not to be identified.

Ellrich said UPS would use management and non-union labour to handle packages containing hospital supplies, medicine and medical equipment, although it was difficult to estimate the volume of material they would be able to transport.

"We will move what packages we can," Ellrich said. Asked if UPS would hire replacement workers, she said, "I have no idea." In the run-up to strike, UPS volume dropped off sharply and the company laid off about 8,000 workers, Ellrich said.
Chief UPS negotiator Dave Murray said the company had "many contingency plans" for the strike although he declined to give any details.
Federal mediator John Calhoun Wells said the strike would affect hundreds of thousands of workers and millions of UPS customers, and the U.S. economy would suffer.
"It's going to have an impact on our nation's economy," Wells told reporters outside his agency's headquarters, where the two sides met for final last-ditch talks to avert the strike.
UPS, which had revenues of $22.4 billion in 1996, ships 3.15 billion parcels and documents annually around the world.

Union officials in Atlanta said striking workers would get $55 a week in strike pay from the union's coffers, and the Teamsters were prepared to get additional funds from the AFL-CIO, the nation's largest federation of trade workers.

Company officials expressed the hope that not all union members would participate in the strike. But union officials have been rallying support at UPS locations around the country this past week and were confident the strike would be honoured.
